symptoms: Bitot's spots (foamy white patches on conjunctiva)
guidance: Treatment: high-dose Vitamin A supplementation (oral) as per WHO schedule—free under government programs. Dietary sources: carrots, sweet potatoes, spinach, pumpkin, mangoes, papaya, eggs, milk, and liver. In severe cases with corneal involvement, urgent ophthalmology referral is needed to prevent blindness.
precautions: Children should receive Vitamin A supplements every 6 months from 6 months to 5 years
Include colorful vegetables and fruits in daily meals
If night blindness is present, seek medical help immediately—do not wait
Pregnant women should not take high-dose Vitamin A (teratogenic risk)—only standard prenatal vitamins
Fortified foods like Vitamin A-fortified oil and milk help prevent deficiency

symptoms: bowed legs (genu varum) or knock-knees (genu valgum)
guidance: Treatment: high-dose Vitamin D (Stoss therapy or daily dosing) plus calcium. Sunlight exposure: 15-30 minutes daily (morning). Dietary sources: fortified milk, egg yolks, fish, and cod liver oil. Prevention: Vitamin D drops for all breastfed infants from 2 weeks of age. Free Vitamin D is available at government health centers.
precautions: Expose child to morning sunlight (7-9 AM) daily
Give Vitamin D supplements to all breastfed infants from birth (400 IU/day)
Include calcium-rich foods: milk, curd, ragi, sesame seeds
Do not give excess Vitamin D without medical monitoring—causes hypercalcemia
If bowed legs or delayed walking, seek pediatric evaluation

symptoms: generalized bone pain (especially hips, lower back, ribs)
muscle weakness (proximal myopathy—difficulty climbing stairs, rising from chair)
guidance: Treatment: Vitamin D supplementation (daily or weekly high-dose) and calcium. Sunlight exposure. Dietary sources: fatty fish, egg yolks, fortified milk. Risk factors: women who cover fully (burqa), elderly, malabsorption. Free testing and supplements at government hospitals.
precautions: Sunlight exposure (hands and face for 15-20 min daily)
Consume calcium-rich foods
Check Vitamin D levels if bone pain is present
Avoid self-prescribing high-dose Vitamin D
If on anticonvulsants or steroids, higher doses may be needed

symptoms: peripheral neuropathy (tingling, numbness in hands and feet)
occurs in fat malabsorption or abetalipoproteinemia
guidance: Vitamin E supplementation (alpha-tocopherol) is treatment. Dietary sources: nuts (almonds, peanuts), seeds (sunflower), spinach, broccoli, and vegetable oils. If due to malabsorption, treat the underlying condition. Neurological symptoms may be irreversible if delayed.
precautions: Include nuts and seeds in daily diet
If on a low-fat diet, ensure adequate vitamin E intake
If neurological symptoms persist, seek neurology evaluation
Do not take high-dose Vitamin E without evidence—risk of bleeding
Check for fat malabsorption if deficiency is severe

symptoms: in newborns: hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (bleeding from umbilical stump, GI bleed, intracranial hemorrhage)
guidance: Treatment: Vitamin K supplementation (oral or injectable). Newborns receive Vitamin K injection at birth (free under government programs). Dietary sources: green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale, fenugreek), broccoli, and fermented foods. If on anticoagulants (warfarin), Vitamin K intake should be consistent.
precautions: All newborns must receive Vitamin K injection at birth—this prevents fatal bleeding
Include green leafy vegetables in regular diet
If on blood thinners, do not suddenly increase Vitamin K intake without doctor's advice
If bleeding is unexplained, seek immediate medical care
Chronic antibiotic use may deplete Vitamin K—consider supplementation

symptoms: DRY BERIBERI: peripheral neuropathy (tingling, weakness, foot drop), muscle wasting, ataxia
WET BERIBERI: heart failure (dyspnea, edema, tachycardia), dilated cardiomyopathy
WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY: confusion, ophthalmoplegia (eye movement paralysis), ataxia, often in alcoholics
infantile beriberi: hoarse cry, vomiting, cyanosis, heart failure
guidance: Treatment: IV or IM thiamine (if severe) or oral thiamine. Dietary sources: whole grains (unpolished rice), legumes, nuts, pork, and fortified cereals. In India, polished rice is a major cause. Wernicke's is a medical emergency—give thiamine before glucose. Free treatment at government hospitals.
precautions: Eat unpolished rice (brown/parboiled) instead of polished white rice
If alcoholic, take thiamine supplements regularly
If Wernicke's suspected (confusion + eye signs), seek emergency care
Do not give glucose without thiamine in suspected Wernicke's
Pregnant and lactating women need extra thiamine

symptoms: inflammation of the corners of the mouth (angular stomatitis)
seborrheic dermatitis (scaly skin around nose, scrotum)
guidance: Treatment: oral riboflavin supplements. Dietary sources: milk, eggs, yogurt, green leafy vegetables, meat, and fortified cereals. Riboflavin is sensitive to light—store milk in opaque containers. Most cases resolve with supplementation.
precautions: Include milk, curd, and green vegetables daily
Store milk away from direct light
If angular stomatitis persists, check for iron and B12 deficiency as well
Do not self-treat—other deficiencies may coexist
If on phenothiazines or tricyclic antidepressants, riboflavin requirement may be higher

symptoms: classic 3 Ds: Dermatitis (rough, scaly rash on sun-exposed areas, hyperpigmentation with peeling), Diarrhea (glossitis, stomatitis, GI upset), Dementia (confusion, memory loss, depression, psychosis)
guidance: Treatment: oral niacinamide (not niacin, which causes flushing). Dietary sources: meat, fish, poultry, eggs, legumes, and niacin-fortified cereals. Corn-based diets (maize) without processing can cause pellagra (bound niacin). Free treatment available. If dementia is present, may need hospitalization.
precautions: If diet is mainly maize, treat corn with alkali (lime water) to release bound niacin
Ensure protein intake (meat, eggs, legumes)
If rash on sun-exposed areas, avoid sun and seek medical care
Do not use high-dose niacin for pellagra—use niacinamide
Pellagra can occur with isoniazid (TB drug) treatment—supplement B3

guidance: Vitamin B5 is widespread in foods; deficiency is very rare except in severe malnutrition. Treatment: oral pantothenic acid. Dietary sources: meat, avocados, broccoli, eggs, whole grains, legumes.
precautions: Rare deficiency—if symptoms persist, check other B vitamins
Include whole grains and vegetables
If on prolonged antibiotics, consider supplementation
Do not take high doses—may cause diarrhea
Balanced diet prevents deficiency

symptoms: can be caused by isoniazid, penicillamine
guidance: Treatment: oral pyridoxine. Dietary sources: chickpeas, poultry, fish, potatoes, bananas, and fortified cereals. If on isoniazid (TB treatment), prophylactic B6 is given. In infants with seizures, IV B6 is diagnostic and therapeutic.
precautions: If on TB treatment (isoniazid), take B6 supplement as prescribed
Include bananas, chickpeas, and potatoes in diet
If taking oral contraceptives, B6 requirement may be higher
Do not self-diagnose B6 deficiency—nerve damage can be irreversible
Consult doctor for dosing

symptoms: scaly, red skin rash around eyes, nose, mouth (seborrheic dermatitis)
guidance: Treatment: oral biotin. Common causes: prolonged raw egg white consumption (avidin binds biotin), certain anticonvulsants, and genetic biotinidase deficiency. Dietary sources: eggs (cooked, not raw), liver, salmon, nuts, seeds, and sweet potatoes.
precautions: Do not consume large amounts of raw egg whites
If on anticonvulsants, consider biotin supplementation
In infants with developmental delay, screen for biotinidase deficiency
Biotin is safe at high doses
Include cooked eggs and nuts in diet

symptoms: megaloblastic anemia (fatigue, pallor, weakness, shortness of breath)
neural tube defects in fetus (spina bifida, anencephaly)
guidance: Treatment: oral folic acid (1-5 mg/day). In pregnancy, 400-600 mcg/day prevents neural tube defects—free IFA tablets are given under government programs. Dietary sources: dark green leafy vegetables (spinach, fenugreek), legumes, citrus fruits, and fortified cereals. For malabsorption, higher doses may be needed.
precautions: All women of childbearing age should take folic acid supplements (400 mcg/day) if planning pregnancy
Do not stop folic acid in pregnancy—prevents birth defects
If anemia is not responding, check B12 as well (giving folic acid alone can mask B12 deficiency)
Include green leafy vegetables daily
If on methotrexate or antiepileptics, higher doses may be needed

symptoms: megaloblastic anemia (fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath)
peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, especially hands and feet)
subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (loss of vibration/position sense, ataxia, weakness)
guidance: Treatment: oral B12 supplements (high dose) or intramuscular injections (cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin)—available free at government hospitals. Dietary sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, and dairy. Strict vegetarians need fortified foods or supplements. Neurological symptoms may be partially reversible if treated early.
precautions: Strict vegetarians and vegans MUST take B12 supplements (at least 2.4 mcg/day)
Do not delay treatment if neurological symptoms are present
If taking metformin long-term, B12 should be checked annually
If anemia is treated with folic acid alone, B12 deficiency can be masked—check both
In Pernicious anemia (autoimmune), lifetime B12 injections are needed

symptoms: in children: irritability, bone pain, pseudoparalysis
guidance: Treatment: oral Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) 300-500 mg/day. Dietary sources: citrus fruits (lemon, orange), amla (Indian gooseberry), guava, tomatoes, and green vegetables. Scurvy is rare but can occur in alcoholics, elderly, or those on severely restricted diets.
precautions: Include fruits and vegetables rich in Vitamin C daily
Amla is an excellent Indian source—consume regularly
If bleeding gums, do not ignore—seek medical help
Smoking increases Vitamin C requirement
Do not take massive doses (>2000 mg/day)—causes diarrhea

guidance: Treatment: oral ferrous sulfate (65 mg elemental iron) 2-3 times daily, with Vitamin C to enhance absorption. For severe anemia, IV iron or blood transfusion. Dietary sources: red meat, poultry, fish, eggs, legumes, green leafy vegetables, and fortified cereals. Free iron supplements are available at PHCs under Anemia Mukt Bharat. Continue for 3-6 months to replenish stores.
precautions: Take iron supplements with Vitamin C (lemon water) to increase absorption
Avoid tea/coffee within 1 hour of iron intake—they block absorption
Do not take iron with calcium supplements—separate by 2 hours
If GI side effects (nausea, constipation), take after meals
Do not self-diagnose—get Hb tested regularly

symptoms: hypothyroidism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin
guidance: Treatment: iodine supplementation (oral iodine, or Lugol's solution in severe cases). Universal salt iodization is the key prevention—use only iodized salt. Seafood is rich in iodine. In pregnant women, iodine requirement is higher—ensure iodized salt and prenatal vitamins containing iodine.
precautions: Use only iodized salt (5 ppm iodine) in daily cooking
Store iodized salt in airtight containers—iodine can evaporate
Do not use non-iodized salt
If goiter is present, check TSH and T4
Pregnant women need adequate iodine—do not avoid salt

symptoms: skin lesions (acrodermatitis enteropathica—vesicular rash around mouth, anus)
guidance: Treatment: oral zinc supplements (20-50 mg/day for 2-3 months). Dietary sources: meat, shellfish, legumes, nuts, seeds, dairy, and whole grains. In children, zinc is given during diarrhea (10-20 mg/day for 14 days) to reduce severity. Free zinc supplements are available under government programs.
precautions: Take zinc supplements with food to reduce GI upset
If on iron supplements, separate zinc and iron doses by 2 hours (competition for absorption)
If using zinc for wound healing, continue until wound closes
Do not take high doses (>40 mg/day) long-term—may cause copper deficiency
Include nuts and seeds in daily diet

symptoms: tingling in fingers and around mouth (hypocalcemia)
guidance: Treatment: calcium supplements (oral calcium carbonate or calcium citrate)—free under some government programs for pregnant women. Dietary sources: milk, curd, paneer, ragi (finger millet), sesame seeds (til), leafy greens, and sardines. Combine with Vitamin D for absorption. For osteoporosis, higher doses (1200 mg/day) are needed.
precautions: Consume calcium-rich foods daily—milk, curd, ragi, sesame seeds
If taking calcium supplements, do not exceed 2000 mg/day (risk of kidney stones)
Take calcium in divided doses (better absorption)
Avoid taking calcium with iron (competition)—separate by 2 hours
If on vitamin D, calcium absorption is enhanced—ensure both

guidance: Treatment: oral magnesium supplements (magnesium citrate, glycinate)—avoid oxide due to poor absorption. Dietary sources: green leafy vegetables, nuts (almonds, cashews), seeds (pumpkin, sunflower), legumes, whole grains, and bananas. Risk factors: alcoholics, diabetics, malabsorption, and diuretic use.
precautions: Include nuts, seeds, and green vegetables daily
If taking magnesium supplements, choose citrate or glycinate for better absorption
Do not exceed 350 mg/day from supplements (diarrhea risk)
If on diuretics or PPIs, consider magnesium monitoring
Hypomagnesemia can cause refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia

symptoms: Keshan disease: cardiomyopathy (enlarged heart, heart failure) in children and women of childbearing age
Kashin-Beck disease: osteoarthropathy (joint pain, enlargement, stiff joints)
thyroid dysfunction (selenium is needed for thyroid hormone metabolism)
guidance: Treatment: oral sodium selenite or selenomethionine supplements. Dietary sources: Brazil nuts, seafood, eggs, meats, and whole grains. In India, selenium levels vary by region. Selenium deficiency is rare but occurs in areas with low soil selenium (e.g., some parts of Northeast India).
precautions: Consume selenium-rich foods—Brazil nuts (1-2 nuts/day is enough), eggs, fish
Do not take high doses (>400 mcg/day)—selenium toxicity (selenosis): garlic breath, hair loss, nail brittleness
If on hemodialysis, supplementation may be needed
Selenium is important for thyroid health—combine with iodine
Check levels if unexplained cardiomyopathy

symptoms: anemia (normocytic or microcytic, unresponsive to iron)
in infants: failure to thrive, developmental delay (Menkes disease)
guidance: Treatment: oral copper supplementation (copper gluconate). Dietary sources: shellfish, liver, nuts, seeds, whole grains, and legumes. Risk factors: malabsorption, gastric bypass surgery, prolonged zinc supplementation (competition), and genetic disorders (Wilson's disease is copper excess, not deficiency).
precautions: If taking high-dose zinc (>50 mg/day), monitor copper levels
Include nuts, shellfish, and liver in diet
If anemia is not responding to iron, check copper
Do not take copper supplements without medical supervision—toxicity is possible
In Menkes disease, copper histidinate injections are needed

symptoms: bone demineralization and poor bone health
guidance: Manganese is a trace mineral. Deficiency is rare. Dietary sources: nuts, seeds, whole grains, leafy greens, tea, and pineapple. Treatment: oral manganese supplementation if confirmed. No RDA established but estimated 2-5 mg/day.
precautions: Whole grains, nuts, and leafy greens provide adequate manganese
Deficiency is extremely rare—do not supplement without confirmed deficiency
Excessive manganese (inhalation in welders) causes neurotoxicity (manganism)
If on TPN (total parenteral nutrition), ensure manganese is included
General balanced diet meets requirements

guidance: Chromium is a trace mineral that enhances insulin action. Deficiency is rare. Treatment: oral chromium picolinate supplements if confirmed. Dietary sources: broccoli, whole grains, meat, nuts, and brewer's yeast. High-dose supplements are not recommended for diabetes without evidence.
precautions: Include whole grains and broccoli in diet
Do not self-medicate with chromium for diabetes—evidence is weak
If taking chromium supplements, do not exceed 50 mcg/day without medical advice
Chromium supplements may cause skin irritation and sleep disturbances
A balanced diet provides adequate chromium

guidance: Molybdenum is a cofactor for enzymes metabolizing sulfur amino acids and uric acid. Deficiency is extremely rare. Dietary sources: legumes, grains, nuts, and leafy greens. Treatment: oral molybdenum supplementation if confirmed.
precautions: Rare deficiency—do not supplement routinely
A balanced diet provides adequate molybdenum
Excess molybdenum can increase uric acid and cause gout-like symptoms
If on TPN, ensure molybdenum is included
No established RDA, adequate intake is 45 mcg/day

guidance: Treatment: oral potassium supplements (potassium chloride) or dietary correction. Dietary sources: bananas, potatoes, sweet potatoes, spinach, beans, and coconut water. Risk factors: diuretics, diarrhea, vomiting, excessive sweating. Severe hypokalemia requires IV potassium.
precautions: Include potassium-rich foods daily—bananas, coconut water, spinach
If taking diuretics, monitor potassium levels
Do not take potassium supplements without checking levels (risk of hyperkalemia)
If on ACE inhibitors or ARBs, potassium levels can rise—monitor
Do not crush or chew potassium tablets—GI irritation

guidance: Treatment: oral phosphate supplements (Fleet enema not for oral). Dietary sources: milk, cheese, meat, fish, nuts, beans, and whole grains. Risk factors: starvation, malabsorption, prolonged antacid use. Often coexists with calcium and Vitamin D deficiency.
precautions: Include dairy and nuts in diet
If on phosphate binders (chronic kidney disease), supplement may be needed
Do not take excessive phosphate—causes hyperphosphatemia
Alcoholism and refeeding syndrome can cause hypophosphatemia—medical supervision
If bone pain, check calcium, phosphorus, and Vitamin D

symptoms: skin and bones appearance (old man face)
guidance: Marasmus is due to overall calorie deficiency. Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation with therapeutic feeding—F-75, F-100, and Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF/Plumpy'Nut). Free at Nutrition Rehabilitation Centers (NRCs) in government hospitals. Refer all SAM children to NRC. Feeding should be gradual to avoid refeeding syndrome.
precautions: Refer to NRC immediately
Do not give high-calorie feeds rapidly—risk of refeeding syndrome
Continue breastfeeding
Monitor for complications (hypothermia, hypoglycemia, infections)
Government provides free therapeutic food

symptoms: skin changes: hyperpigmentation, desquamation, fissures (flaky paint dermatosis)
potbelly (protuberant abdomen due to fatty liver)
guidance: Kwashiorkor is due to protein deficiency despite adequate calories. Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation with high-protein foods and therapeutic milk (F-75, F-100). Free treatment at NRCs. Severe cases may need IV albumin. Correct electrolyte imbalances (potassium, magnesium).
precautions: Do not give high-protein loads rapidly—precipitates complications
Monitor for infection and sepsis
Begin with F-75 then F-100
Continue breastfeeding
Refer to NRC immediately—do not treat at home

guidance: Mixed form—most severe PEM. Requires urgent hospitalization at NRC. Therapeutic feeding (F-75, F-100, RUTF). Correct electrolyte abnormalities and treat infections. Close monitoring of weight gain and edema resolution.
precautions: Hospitalize immediately
Gradual nutritional rehabilitation
Monitor for refeeding syndrome
Treat infections aggressively
Long-term follow-up for catch-up growth

guidance: SAM is a medical emergency. Treatment: community-based or facility-based management with RUTF (Plumpy'Nut) under government programs. If complications (fever, severe edema, not eating), refer to NRC. Free treatment under NHM. All SAM children should be screened for TB and HIV.
precautions: MUAC screening at Anganwadi centers
If MUAC < 11.5 cm, refer immediately
Do not give home remedies—need therapeutic food
Monitor for weight gain (minimum 5 g/kg/day)
Deworming and Vitamin A supplementation are part of treatment

guidance: MAM is managed with supplementary feeding (Take-Home Rations) provided at Anganwadi centers. Counseling on dietary diversification, hygiene, and feeding practices. Monitor monthly for progress.
precautions: Attend regular Anganwadi visits
Take the supplementary food given
Continue breastfeeding
Ensure handwashing before meals
If child develops edema, refer to NRC

guidance: Stunting results from prolonged undernutrition, starting in utero. The first 1000 days are critical. Interventions: maternal nutrition during pregnancy, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, diverse complementary feeding (ragi, dal, eggs, vegetables), growth monitoring at Anganwadi. Stunting is largely irreversible after age 2 but can be prevented.
precautions: Measure height and weight monthly at Anganwadi
Ensure mother's nutrition during pregnancy
Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months
Introduce diverse foods at 6 months
Vaccination and deworming are essential

symptoms: may be wasted, stunted, or both
guidance: Underweight is a composite indicator. Management: dietary counseling, supplementary nutrition (Anganwadi), deworming, and regular growth monitoring. Address underlying causes (malabsorption, infection, inadequate feeding).
precautions: Regular growth monitoring
Ensure calorie and protein intake
Deworming every 6 months
Treat infections promptly
Take advantage of Anganwadi nutrition supplementation

guidance: Wasting indicates acute, recent weight loss due to food scarcity or illness. Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation (RUTF if severe), treatment of underlying infection, and dietary counseling. Prevention: adequate feeding during illness, ORS for diarrhea, and continued feeding.
precautions: Continue feeding during illness
Give extra nutrition after illness (catch-up growth)
If MUAC < 12.5 cm, seek medical care
Monitor weight weekly
Vitamin A supplementation

symptoms: acanthosis nigricans (dark skin folds, insulin resistance)
guidance: Obesity is a chronic disease. Management: lifestyle modification—calorie-controlled diet (reduced refined carbs, sugars, saturated fats), increased physical activity (at least 150 min/week of moderate exercise), and behavioral therapy. Pharmacotherapy (orlistat, GLP-1 agonists) and bariatric surgery for severe cases (BMI > 35 with comorbidities). Free obesity clinics at some government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid crash diets—sustainable weight loss is 0.5-1 kg/week
Exercise regularly—walking, swimming, cycling
Reduce screen time
Eat more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
If BMI > 35 with diabetes or hypertension, consult a specialist

symptoms: increased waist circumference (>90 cm in men, >80 cm in women)
guidance: Overweight is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease. Intervention: lifestyle changes—healthy diet (reduce calories, processed foods), regular exercise, and portion control. Even 5-10% weight loss improves metabolic parameters. Free BMI screening at PHCs.
precautions: Monitor waist circumference (central obesity is more dangerous)
Eat a diet rich in fiber and low in refined carbohydrates
Exercise 30-45 minutes daily
Avoid sugary beverages
Regular BP and blood sugar screening

symptoms: central obesity (waist circumference ≥ 90 cm male, ≥ 80 cm female)
low HDL (<40 mg/dL male, <50 mg/dL female)
guidance: Metabolic syndrome increases the risk of diabetes and heart disease. Treatment: lifestyle intervention—weight loss, dietary changes (Mediterranean/DASH diet), increased exercise. Pharmacotherapy for individual components (statins, antihypertensives, metformin). Free NCD screening at PHCs.
precautions: Lose weight—5-10% reduction
Follow DASH diet (low salt, high fruits/vegetables)
Regular aerobic exercise (30-45 min/day)
Monitor BP, lipids, and blood sugar annually
If three criteria are present, treat aggressively

guidance: NAFLD is the hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome. Treatment: lifestyle modification—weight loss (7-10% of body weight) is the most effective. Dietary changes: reduce fructose, refined carbs, and saturated fats. Regular exercise. No specific drug currently approved (vitamin E, pioglitazone for selected cases).
precautions: Weight loss is the cornerstone
Avoid sugary drinks and processed foods
Regular exercise (at least 150 min/week)
If diabetic, control blood sugar
Monitor liver enzymes and ultrasound annually

guidance: Diagnosis: tissue transglutaminase IgA (ttg IgA) and duodenal biopsy. Treatment: strict lifelong gluten-free diet (avoid wheat, barley, rye, and oats cross-contaminated). Free follow-up at government hospitals. Nutritional supplements for deficiencies (iron, B12, calcium, Vitamin D).
precautions: Strict gluten-free diet for life
Avoid cross-contamination (separate utensils)
Read food labels carefully
Take calcium and Vitamin D supplements
Annual follow-up for nutritional status and bone density

symptoms: occurring 30 minutes to 2 hours after consuming dairy products
guidance: Diagnosis: lactose hydrogen breath test or trial elimination. Management: reduce or avoid lactose-containing foods (milk, ice cream, soft cheeses). Lactase enzyme supplements can be taken with dairy. Hard cheeses and yogurt are often better tolerated. Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation is essential to prevent deficiency.
precautions: Choose lactose-free milk or plant-based alternatives
Take lactase enzyme with dairy
Hard cheese (cheddar, parmesan) has less lactose
Ensure adequate calcium intake from non-dairy sources (leafy greens, almonds, fortified foods)
Do not avoid dairy completely without medical advice

symptoms: symptoms occur within minutes to 2 hours of eating the offending food
guidance: Common triggers: peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, eggs, milk, soy, wheat. Diagnosis: skin prick test, specific IgE, or oral food challenge (under supervision). Treatment: strict avoidance; emergency epinephrine (EpiPen) for anaphylaxis. Carry a medical alert bracelet.
precautions: Identify and strictly avoid the allergen
Read food labels carefully
Carry an EpiPen if prescribed
Inform restaurants and family about allergy
If anaphylaxis occurs, use EpiPen and call 108 immediately

guidance: Diagnosis: trial elimination of cow's milk from maternal diet (if breastfeeding) or switch to extensively hydrolyzed formula or amino acid-based formula. For breastfed infants, mother eliminates all dairy. Symptoms usually resolve within 2-4 weeks. Government hospitals provide free formula for severe cases.
precautions: If breastfeeding, mother should eliminate dairy
Use hydrolyzed formula if formula-fed (available at government hospitals for prescription)
Do not give soy formula if also soy allergy
Reintroduce milk gradually after 1 year if tolerated
Monitor growth and development

guidance: Mild-moderate: ORS solution (1 packet in 1 liter clean water)—free at government facilities. Sip slowly. Continue eating light meals. Severe dehydration (vomiting, unable to drink, confusion) needs IV fluids at hospital. Prevention: drink enough water daily (2-3 liters), more in hot weather or with diarrhea.
precautions: Drink clean water regularly—do not wait for thirst
Use ORS for diarrhea or vomiting
Avoid sugary drinks (worsen dehydration)
If unable to keep fluids down, seek hospital care
Elderly and children are at higher risk—monitor closely

symptoms: can occur with excessive water intake without electrolytes (e.g., marathon runners)
guidance: Treatment: fluid restriction, sodium supplements, and treatment of underlying cause. In severe (<120 mEq/L), IV hypertonic saline is given. Prevention: ensure adequate salt intake, especially in hot climates and with heavy sweating. Do not drink large amounts of plain water without food.
precautions: Do not overhydrate with plain water without food
If sweating heavily, add salt to food or use ORS
If on diuretics, monitor sodium levels
If confusion or seizures, seek emergency care
Do not use salt tablets without supervision

guidance: Treatment: gradual fluid replacement (water or IV dextrose). Prevention: reduce salt intake (<5 g/day). Avoid processed foods, pickles, papad, and salty snacks. In children, avoid salty foods. If taking oral rehydration, ensure correct dilution.
precautions: Reduce salt in cooking
Avoid processed and packaged foods (high salt)
Drink adequate water
If on tube feeding, monitor sodium
If thirst is excessive, check sodium level

category: Hyperkalemia (High Potassium) – Dietary Excess or Renal Failure
guidance: Emergency if ECG changes or K > 6.5 mEq/L. Treatment: calcium gluconate (cardioprotection), insulin + glucose, sodium bicarbonate, and potassium binders. Prevention: avoid high-potassium foods if renal failure (bananas, potatoes, coconut water, spinach, oranges). Dialysis if needed.
precautions: If chronic kidney disease, restrict potassium-rich foods
Do not use salt substitutes (KCl)
If on ACE inhibitors/ARBs, monitor potassium
If palpitations or weakness, seek emergency care
Regular blood tests if at risk

guidance: Treatment: oral potassium supplements (KCl) or high-potassium diet. Dietary sources: bananas, coconut water, oranges, potatoes, spinach. In severe (<3.0 mEq/L), IV potassium is needed. Prevention: ensure adequate intake, especially with diarrhea or diuretic use.
precautions: Eat potassium-rich foods daily
If taking diuretics, consider potassium supplementation
Do not crush sustained-release potassium tablets
If muscle weakness or palpitations, check potassium
Coconut water is an excellent source

symptoms: Chvostek sign (facial twitching), Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm)
guidance: Treatment: oral calcium supplements (calcium carbonate or citrate) and Vitamin D to enhance absorption. Severe (<7.5 mg/dL) needs IV calcium gluconate. Dietary sources: milk, curd, ragi, sesame seeds. Chronic hypocalcemia may indicate hypoparathyroidism or malabsorption.
precautions: Ensure adequate calcium and Vitamin D intake
If muscle cramps or tingling, check calcium
Do not take calcium with iron (separate by 2 hours)
If on PPIs long-term, calcium absorption may be impaired
Monitor kidney stones with high-dose calcium

category: Hypercalcemia (High Calcium) – Excess Vitamin D or Calcium
symptoms: can occur with excessive Vitamin D or calcium intake
guidance: Treatment: hydration (IV fluids), diuretics (furosemide), calcitonin, and corticosteroids. Identify and remove the cause (e.g., stop supplements). Prevention: do not exceed recommended doses of Vitamin D and calcium.
precautions: Do not take high-dose Vitamin D or calcium without medical indication
Stay hydrated
If kidney stones, check calcium levels
Monitor for hypercalcemia in tuberculosis or sarcoidosis
Seek care for persistent nausea and confusion

guidance: Diagnosis: serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, genetic testing (HFE). Treatment: therapeutic phlebotomy (regular blood removal) is the mainstay. Dietary: avoid iron supplements, vitamin C (increases absorption), and reduce intake of red meat. Alcohol should be avoided (increases iron absorption and liver damage).
precautions: Avoid iron supplements and multivitamins with iron
Limit red meat intake
Avoid Vitamin C supplements with meals (increases iron absorption)
Do not consume alcohol
If diagnosed, family members should be screened

category: Wilson's Disease – Copper Overload – Dietary Management
symptoms: neurological: tremors, dystonia, speech difficulties, personality changes
guidance: Treatment: chelating agents (penicillamine, trientine) and zinc acetate. Dietary: reduce copper-rich foods (liver, shellfish, nuts, chocolate, mushrooms) during initial treatment. Maintain lifelong therapy. Liver transplant in severe cases. Genetic counseling.
precautions: Avoid copper-rich foods (liver, shellfish, nuts, mushrooms, chocolate)
Use copper-free water pipes if possible
Do not stop chelation therapy—causes deterioration
Regular monitoring of liver function and copper levels
If neurological symptoms, seek urgent care

guidance: Treatment: oral magnesium supplements (citrate, glycinate). Dietary sources: nuts, seeds, leafy greens, legumes, whole grains, bananas. In severe or malabsorption, IV magnesium. Prevention: include magnesium-rich foods daily.
precautions: Include nuts, seeds, and green vegetables daily
If on PPIs or diuretics, monitor magnesium
Do not take magnesium oxide (poor absorption)—choose citrate or glycinate
If muscle cramps persist, check magnesium
Excessive magnesium causes diarrhea

guidance: Treatment: supplementation with linoleic acid (safflower oil, sunflower oil) and alpha-linolenic acid (flaxseed oil). Dietary sources: vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, fish. Deficiency is rare except in severe fat malabsorption or TPN without lipids.
precautions: Include vegetable oils, nuts, and seeds in diet
